h.en: Why Use Utility Classes and How They Are Named

body.en:
So far every page had to mix Bootstrap components with hand-written CSS for every small change: a little more space here, a border there. Bootstrap utilities are tiny, single-purpose CSS classes that add one style (margin, colour, border...) directly in the HTML.

Benefits of using utilities

  • No custom CSS files for small fixes - the same class works in every project.
  • Faster development: spacing, sizes and colours are set while writing the markup.
  • Consistent look: all values come from Bootstrap's scale (0-5), so the design stays uniform.
  • Responsive by default: many utilities exist in breakpoint versions like p-md-4.
  • Small and safe: using them does not add extra size to the downloaded CSS beyond bootstrap.css itself.

Naming rules

  • Spacing follows {property}{sides}-{size}: mt-3 = margin-top of size 3.
  • Other families follow {utility}-{value}, e.g. bg-primary, rounded-pill, shadow-lg.
  • Responsive versions insert the breakpoint: {utility}-{bp}-{value}, e.g. d-md-flex.
<div class="p-3 m-2">all sides</div>
<div class="pt-0 pb-4">top / bottom</div>
<div class="ps-2 me-auto">start / end</div>
<div class="px-3 py-1">x = left+right, y = top+bottom</div>
<div class="w-50 mx-auto">centre block</div>
<div class="d-flex gap-2">space between items</div>
<div class="mt-0 mt-md-3">responsive spacing</div>

h.en: The Utility Families at a Glance

body.en:
The syllabus lists the utility families together; this topic maps each family to a typical class and use:

  • Spacing - margin, padding, gap (w5_1).
  • Sizing - width, height, viewport, ratio (w5_2).
  • Display and visibility - show, hide, flow (w5_3).
  • Positioning - corners, centre, badges, z-index (w5_4).
  • Flexbox - rows, columns, alignment (w5_5).
  • Border - sides, colour, width, rounding (w5_6).
  • Background - fills, gradient, subtle, opacity (w5_7).
  • Opacity, overflow, shadow - transparency, clipping, depth (w5_8).
  • All families become responsive with a breakpoint infix (w5_9).

The diagram is the complete cheat-sheet table; learn the family names for theory questions.

Sizing utilities set width and height as a percentage of the parent (or fit content):

  • Width: w-25 w-50 w-75 w-100 w-auto; maximum mw-100.
  • Height: h-25 ... h-100, h-auto, mh-100. A percentage height works only if the parent has a height.
  • Viewport: vw-100, vh-100, min-vh-100 for full-screen sections.
  • Ratio: .ratio with ratio-1x1, ratio-4x3, ratio-16x9, ratio-21x9 keeps videos and iframes in proportion on any screen.
<img src="photo.jpg" class="w-50">   <!-- 50% of parent -->
<div class="w-25 w-50 w-75 w-100 w-auto"></div>
<div class="h-100" style="height: 200px">parent needs height</div>
<img class="mw-100">  <!-- never wider than screen -->
<section class="vh-100">full-screen section</section>
<div class="ratio ratio-16x9">
  <video> or <iframe>           <!-- keeps 16:9 shape -->
</div>

Try the live example: blue bars at 25-100% width, green bars at 25-100% height, a banner limited by mw-100 and a 16:9 video box.

Display utilities control how an element takes part in the layout. Format: d-{value} or d-{breakpoint}-{value}.

  • Values: none, inline, inline-block, block, table, flex, inline-flex, grid.
  • Responsive hiding: d-md-none hides from 768 px up; d-none d-md-block shows only from 768 px. Combine them for different phone and desktop layouts.
  • Visibility is different: .invisible hides but keeps the space in the layout; d-none removes the space completely.
  • .visually-hidden keeps content for screen readers only.
  • .d-print-* controls printing, e.g. hide a Print button on paper.
<span class="d-block">              span -> block
<div class="d-inline-block w-25">  sized inline
<div class="d-none d-md-block">    hidden below 768px
<div class="d-md-none">            only below 768px
<span class="invisible">           hidden, keeps space
<span class="visually-hidden">     screen readers only
<button class="d-print-none">      hidden when printing

The live example shows a breakpoint badge that always displays the current screen size - the trick used in many real websites.

Position utilities place elements without writing CSS:

  • position-*: static, relative, absolute, fixed, sticky.
  • Edge placement: top-0, bottom-0, start-0, end-0, also 50 and 100 (percentages).
  • translate-middle shifts the element back by half of its own size, so top-50 start-50 translate-middle centres it exactly inside a position-relative parent. The classic badge on a button uses top-0 start-100 translate-middle.
  • z-index: z-n1, z-0 ... z-3 control which overlapping element is in front.
  • Shortcuts: .fixed-top, .fixed-bottom, .sticky-top.
<div class="position-relative">
  <span class="position-absolute top-0 start-0">
  <span class="position-absolute bottom-0 end-0">
  <span class="position-absolute top-50 start-50
        translate-middle">exact centre</span>
  <span class="position-absolute top-0 start-100
        translate-middle badge bg-danger">5</span>
</div>
<!-- edges: 0, 50, 100  = % of the parent -->
<!-- stack order: z-n1 z-0 z-1 z-2 z-3 -->

Flexbox lays items out in one direction with automatic spacing and alignment. Add d-flex to any container and tune it with utilities:

  • Direction: flex-row (default), flex-column, and *-reverse versions; responsive with flex-md-row.
  • Main axis (along the direction) is controlled by justify-content-start / center / end / between / around / evenly.
  • Cross axis by align-items-start / center / end / baseline / stretch; align-self-* overrides one item, align-content-* spaces wrapped lines.
  • Wrapping: flex-wrap sends extra items to a new line.
  • Per item: order-0..5, flex-grow-1 (fill free space), ms-auto (push apart).
<div class="d-flex flex-column flex-md-row gap-2
     justify-content-between align-items-center">
  <div class="order-md-2">A</div>
  <div class="flex-grow-1">B takes free space</div>
  <div class="ms-md-auto">C pushed right</div>
</div>

The live example has drop-downs for both axes and a stacked-on-phone / row-on-desktop layout - the standard pattern for headers and cards.

• Add: border, border-top, border-end, border-bottom, border-start.
  • Remove: border-0, border-top-0 ...
  • Colour: border-primary, border-danger, border-success-subtle ...; set border first (it creates the edge), then colour it.
  • Width: border-1 to border-5; opacity: border-opacity-10/25/50/75.
  • Rounding: rounded, rounded-0 ... rounded-5 (corner size), rounded-top/-end/-bottom/-start (one side), rounded-pill (capsule), rounded-circle (needs equal width and height).
<div class="border">, border-top, border-end, ...
<div class="border border-top-0">   remove one side
<div class="border border-danger border-2">
<div class="border border-success border-opacity-25">
<div class="rounded-0 rounded rounded-3 rounded-5">
<div class="rounded-top rounded-bottom">
<div class="rounded-pill px-4">       pill / capsule
<div class="rounded-circle">          circle (w == h)

• Fills: bg-primary, -secondary, -success, -danger, -warning, -info, -light, -dark, -white, -transparent, bg-body, bg-body-secondary/-tertiary.
  • text-bg-* sets the fill AND a readable text colour together - ideal for badges and dark headers.
  • bg-gradient adds a subtle light-to-dark gradient over any fill.
  • Subtle colours: bg-*-subtle with text-*-emphasis for soft highlight panels (Bootstrap 5.3).
  • bg-opacity-* fades only the background, leaving text solid.
  • Text: text-primary ... text-body-secondary (muted), text-white-50; links: link-* and link-underline-opacity-0.
<div class="bg-primary text-white">
<div class="bg-primary bg-gradient">  light gradient
<span class="badge text-bg-warning">  bg + text colour
<div class="bg-success-subtle text-success-emphasis">
<div class="bg-success bg-opacity-25"> fade only the bg
<p class="text-primary">, text-body-secondary
<a class="link-danger"> link colour

Background and text colour utilities are not responsive - a colour stays the same on all screen sizes.

• Opacity opacity-0/25/50/75/100 makes the whole element - including its text and children - transparent. Use bg-opacity-* when only the background should fade.
  • Overflow decides what happens when content is bigger than its box: overflow-auto (scroll bar when needed), overflow-hidden (clip it, e.g. to keep round corners on an image), overflow-visible (default), overflow-scroll (always scroll bars); single direction with overflow-x-* / overflow-y-*. Requires a fixed height/width on the box.
  • Shadow gives depth: shadow-none shadow-sm shadow shadow-lg; very common on cards, fixed navbars and FAB buttons.
<img class="opacity-50">          element half visible
<div class="overflow-auto" style="height:100px">
  scroll bar only when needed</div>
<div class="overflow-hidden">     cut off, no scroll
<div class="overflow-x-auto">     sideways scroll
<div class="shadow-sm shadow shadow-lg shadow-none">

Bootstrap is mobile first: a class without a breakpoint applies to all screens, and a class with a breakpoint overrides it from that width up:

  • {utility}-{bp}-{value} where bp = sm (576), md (768), lg (992), xl (1200), xxl (1400 px).
  • d-none d-md-block: hidden on phones, visible from tablets. flex-column flex-md-row: stack on phones, row from tablets.
  • Responsive families: display, flex (direction, justify, align, order), spacing, text alignment (text-md-start), float (float-md-end), sticky (sticky-md-top) and grid columns.
  • Not responsive: width/height (w-50), colours, borders, shadows - add your own small media-query class like .w-md-auto in the live page, or generate them with the Sass utility API.
<div class="text-center text-md-start">
<div class="d-flex flex-column flex-md-row">
<div class="p-2 p-md-4 mt-1 mt-lg-3">
<span class="d-none d-md-inline">desktop only</span>
<span class="float-md-end">        floats right >=768px
<!-- pattern: {utility}-{sm|md|lg|xl|xxl}-{value} -->

h.en: Practical 22: Header and Footer with Only Utility Classes

body.en:
The practical asks for a tourism website header and footer built only with utility classes (no custom CSS beyond one helper). The live program shows the keys:

  • Header layout is pure flexbox: d-flex flex-wrap align-items-center justify-content-between gap-2.
  • Responsive order: order-3 order-md-2 puts the menu on a second line on phones and between logo and button on desktops.
  • Colours and depth: bg-primary bg-gradient, shadow, text-white-50, link-light.
  • Footer grid: col-12 col-md-5 etc. give 1 column on a phone and 3 on a desktop; border-top border-secondary separates the copyright line.
  • Typography classes do the text design: fs-5, fw-bold, small, text-body-secondary.
<header class="bg-primary bg-gradient text-white shadow">
  <div class="container d-flex flex-wrap align-items-center
       justify-content-between gap-2 py-2">
    <a class="d-flex align-items-center gap-2 ...">logo</a>
    <ul class="nav order-3 order-md-2 ...">links</ul>
    <a class="btn btn-warning btn-sm rounded-pill
       order-2 order-md-3">Book now</a>
  </div>
</header>

h.en: Why Customize Bootstrap and the Five Levels

body.en:
Default Bootstrap is safe but generic - every site looks the same blue. Customization makes the framework match your own brand and your own components.

Benefits of customizing Bootstrap

  • Brand identity - your colours, fonts and corner styles instead of defaults.
  • Smaller CSS - keep only the colours and utilities you use.
  • Design that updates itself: change one variable and every component follows, no class-by-class patching.
  • Consistency: custom values become part of the same utility system (btn-brand, bg-brand).

The five levels (simple -> powerful)

  1. CSS variables on :root - change at runtime, no tools needed.
  2. Sass variables before the import - change the defaults for the whole library ($primary, $border-radius...).
  3. Sass maps and the utility API - add your own colours and utilities.
  4. Component variables - tune one component ($card-border-radius) without touching global defaults.
  5. Themes - a packaged set of levels 1-4 that gives the site a complete identity.

The live program demonstrates level 1: overriding --bs-primary and friends on :root.

<style>
  :root {
    --bs-primary: #7b1fa2;
    --bs-primary-rgb: 123, 31, 162;
    --bs-body-font-family: Georgia, serif;
    --bs-border-radius: 1rem;
  }
  /* buttons use their own variables */
  .btn-primary { --bs-btn-bg: var(--bs-primary); }
</style>

Bootstrap is written in Sass, and its defaults are variables with !default - meaning use this value only if nothing else was set. That single feature powers the whole customization system:

  1. Create your own file, e.g. scss/_custom.scss.
  2. Set variables BEFORE the import line: $primary: #198754;, $border-radius: 0.75rem; - your values replace the !default values.
  3. Import Bootstrap: @import "bootstrap/scss/bootstrap";.
  4. Compile: dart-sass scss/_custom.scss css/custom.css (or an npm script).
  5. Link custom.css instead of bootstrap.css on every page.
  • Files starting with an underscore (_variables.scss) are partials - they are merged into the build, not compiled alone.
  • Recompile whenever a variable changes; editors like VS Code can rebuild on save.
  • The live program (Practical 23) shows the Sass source and the compiled result side by side as you change the brand colour and corner radius.
// scss/_custom.scss - variables BEFORE the import
$primary: #198754;
$border-radius: 0.75rem;
@import "bootstrap/scss/bootstrap";

// build it:
// dart-sass scss/_custom.scss css/custom.css
// page links css/custom.css instead of bootstrap.css

Every component also has its own Sass variables, so one component can be restyled without changing the global defaults:

  • Examples: $card-border-radius, $card-box-shadow, $btn-border-radius, $navbar-padding-y, $modal-content-border-width. They are documented at the bottom of each component's page.
  • Set them before the import, compile, and that component alone keeps the new shape everywhere.

Sass maps: your own theme colours

  • Bootstrap's colours live in the $theme-colors map. map-merge adds colours; Bootstrap then automatically creates btn-brand, alert-brand, bg-brand, text-brand ... with correct hover and contrast.
  • map-remove drops colours you never use, shrinking the compiled CSS.
  • The utility API works the same way: its $utilities map can be extended to generate e.g. responsive width classes (w-md-25).
// component variables (before import)
$card-border-radius: 1rem;
$btn-border-radius: 0.5rem;

// add a brand colour to the Sass map:
$theme-colors: map-merge($theme-colors,
               ("brand": #7b1fa2));
// -> creates btn-brand, alert-brand, bg-brand, ...
// shrink output: map-remove($theme-colors, "cyan", ...)

The live program (Practical 24a) lets you drag the card corner radius and shows the exact Sass source that produces the result.

A theme is a complete, documented set of variable and component overrides that gives the site its identity.

  • Bootstrap 5.3 ships two built-in colour modes: light and dark. Set data-bs-theme="dark" on <html> (whole page) or on any section - every component adapts automatically.
  • Custom themes are built by overriding CSS variables under your own [data-bs-theme="name"] selector (as in the demo), or by compiling a separate Sass build per theme.
  • Packaged themes (Bootswatch, Start Bootstrap) are exactly such override sets - install one and its classes are still plain Bootstrap.

Rules for themable markup

  • Style with semantic classes: text-bg-primary, btn-primary, bg-body - never hard-coded hex colours.
  • Then a theme switch only changes variables, and the whole site flips cleanly - as the dropdown in the live program (Practical 24b) shows.
<html data-bs-theme="dark">   <!-- whole page dark -->
<section data-bs-theme="dark"> <!-- one section dark -->

<style>
/* own theme = its own set of variables */
[data-bs-theme="brand"] {
  --bs-body-bg: #f3ecfa;
  --bs-body-color: #3c2352;
  --bs-primary: #7b2cd9;
  --bs-border-radius: 0.9rem;
}
</style>

title.en: Spacing utilities: margin, padding and gap

code.en:
Spacing: {property}{sides}-{size}

Padding sizes p-0 to p-5

p-0
p-1
p-2
p-3
p-4
p-5

Sides: t, b, s (start), e (end), x, y

mt-3 ms-5
my-3 mx-auto (centred)

Gap between flex items

gap-3
gap-3
gap-3

Responsive spacing

p-1 on phones, p-md-5 from 768 px

programs.out:
A row of blue boxes with increasing padding labelled p-0 to p-5.
In a light yellow area: one box pushed down and right (mt-3 ms-5) and a 200 px box centred with mx-auto.
Three green boxes separated by gap-3. A blue box with small padding on a phone and large padding (p-md-5) on a wider screen.

expl.en:
• Format: {property}{sides}-{size}. Property: m (margin) or p (padding).
  • Sides: t top, b bottom, s start (left), e end (right), x left + right, y top + bottom, none = all sides. (Bootstrap 4 used l and r.)
  • Sizes: 0, 1 (0.25rem), 2 (0.5rem), 3 (1rem), 4 (1.5rem), 5 (3rem), and auto for margins.
  • mx-auto centres a block element that has a width.
  • gap-*, row-gap-*, column-gap-* set the space between flex or grid items.
  • Responsive: {property}{sides}-{bp}-{size}, e.g. p-md-5, mt-lg-0.

title.en: Sizing utilities: width, height and ratio

code.en:
Width (relative to parent)

w-25
w-50

Height

h-25

programs.out:
Four blue bars that fill 25%, 50%, 75% and 100% of the grey box, plus a dark w-auto box only as wide as its text.
Four green bars that are 25% to 100% as tall as the 120 px box.
A wide banner image that never gets wider than the screen (mw-100), and a dark box with a 16:9 shape, half the page wide.

expl.en:
• Width: w-25, w-50, w-75, w-100, w-auto, percentages of the parent's width.
  • Height: h-25 to h-100, h-auto; percentages of the parent's height (the parent needs a height).
  • Max: mw-100 (max-width: 100%), mh-100.
  • Viewport: vw-100, vh-100, min-vw-100, min-vh-100 (e.g. a full-screen landing section).
  • Ratio: .ratio .ratio-16x9 (also 1x1, 4x3, 21x9) keeps an aspect ratio for videos and iframes; the child fills the box.

title.en: Display and visibility utilities with a breakpoint indicator

code.en:
Display and visibility

Screen: xs sm md lg xl+

Display values

span with d-block
div d-inline
inline-block

Responsive show / hide

Phone view: only on screens below 768 px
Desktop view: only from 768 px

Visibility

A
B
C

B is invisible but keeps its space. Read by screen readers only.

programs.out:
A dark badge shows the current screen size, e.g. "Screen: xs" on a phone or "Screen: xl+" on a large monitor.
A blue full-width span, two yellow inline boxes, a blue "Phone view" alert on small screens or a green "Desktop view" alert on wide screens.
Boxes A and C are red with an empty gap where the invisible box B is.

expl.en:
• Display: .d-{value} or .d-{bp}-{value}; values none, inline, inline-block, block, grid, inline-grid, table, flex, inline-flex.
  • Responsive hiding: d-none d-md-block = hidden below md; d-md-none = visible only below md. The badge uses this to show the current breakpoint.
  • Visibility: .invisible hides but keeps the space (visibility: hidden); .visible shows it.
  • .visually-hidden hides content from the screen but not from screen readers.
  • Print: .d-print-none, .d-print-block control what is printed.

programs.out:
A grey box with labels in all four corners (blue at the top, green at the bottom) and a red "centre" label exactly in the middle.
A dark "Messages" button with a red round badge "5" on its top-right corner.
Three overlapping coloured boxes; the blue z-3 box is on top of both others.

expl.en:
• Position: position-static, -relative, -absolute, -fixed, -sticky.
  • Edges: top-, bottom-, start-, end- with values 0, 50, 100 (%).
  • translate-middle moves the element back by 50% of its own size, so top-50 start-50 translate-middle centres it exactly. Also translate-middle-x and -y.
  • An absolute element is placed relative to the nearest position-relative parent.
  • z-index: z-n1, z-0, z-1, z-2, z-3 (Bootstrap 5.3); higher numbers are drawn on top.
  • Shortcuts: .fixed-top, .fixed-bottom, .sticky-top, .sticky-bottom.

  • Overflow only matters when the element has a fixed height or width.
  • Shadow: shadow-none, shadow-sm, shadow, shadow-lg; used on cards, navbars and buttons to give depth.

On a phone: the teacher's photo, name and department are stacked and centred, and the Contact button is full width.
From 768 px: photo, text and button are in one row, text is left-aligned, and the button is normal width. From 992 px the padding becomes larger.
The green "float-md-end" text moves to the right side from md. The badge shows the current breakpoint.

expl.en:
• Most utilities have responsive versions with a breakpoint infix: {utility}-{bp}-{value}, where bp = sm, md, lg, xl, xxl.
  • Bootstrap is mobile first: the class without a breakpoint applies to all screens; the md class overrides it from 768 px up.
  • Responsive utilities include display (d-md-flex), flex (flex-md-row, justify-content-lg-between), spacing (p-lg-4), text alignment (text-md-start), float (float-md-end), sticky (sticky-md-top) and grid columns.
  • Width, height, colour and border utilities are not responsive by default; a small media query (like .w-md-auto here) or the Sass utility API adds them.

A notice card with a "New" badge, a blue button and a link.
Click ":root variables overridden": the badge, the button and the link turn purple, the corners become very round, and the font changes to a serif font; the CSS block below shows the new variable values.
Click "Default Bootstrap" to go back to the blue default look.

expl.en:
• Bootstrap's colours, fonts, borders and spacing variables are stored as CSS custom properties on :root, e.g. --bs-primary, --bs-font-sans-serif, --bs-border-radius.
  • Every component and utility (btn-primary, text-bg-primary, rounded...) is built on these variables, so overriding them on :root changes the whole site at once — no new CSS per component.
  • For colour variables, also override the RGB twin (--bs-primary-rgb); it is used for transparency (shadows, opacity).
  • Buttons use their own variables (--bs-btn-bg ...); point them at --bs-primary or set them, so buttons follow the theme too.
  • Overrides can also be scoped to one element instead of :root to restyle just that section.
  • CSS variables are the simplest level of customization: no build tools needed, works at runtime. For deeper changes Sass is used (next programs).

• Bootstrap is written in Sass. Its defaults live in _variables.scss ($primary, $secondary, $border-radius, $font-family-sans-serif, grid breakpoints...).
  • To customize, create your own file, set the variables before the import line, then import Bootstrap's Sass. Sass variables with !default in Bootstrap yield to your values.
  • Change the brand colour or corner radius here and see the compiled result instantly; the left panel shows the exact Sass source that produces it.
  • Compile with dart-sass main.scss custom.css (or npm + sass) and link custom.css instead of the default bootstrap.css. Every component uses the new defaults without touching the HTML.

  • Set them before importing Bootstrap to reshape only that component (like the card above), while the global $border-radius stays untouched.
  • Component variables are documented at the bottom of each component's docs page.
  • Sass maps: extend $theme-colors with map-merge to add a brand colour; it automatically creates utilities and component variants (btn-brand, alert-brand, text-brand, bg-brand).
  • Remove unused colours with map-remove to shrink the compiled CSS.

expl.en:
• A theme is a complete set of variable and component overrides that gives the site its own identity (colours, radius, shadows, fonts).
  • Bootstrap 5.3 adds colour modes: set data-bs-theme="dark" on <html> or on any section to switch it to dark; data-bs-theme="light" is the default. All components react automatically.
  • Custom themes are made by overriding CSS variables under your own [data-bs-theme="name"] selector (as in this program), or by compiling a custom Sass build per theme.
  • Keep theming at variable level: write markup with semantic classes (text-bg-primary, btn-primary), never hard-coded hex colours, and themes switch cleanly.
  • Ready-made themes (Bootswatch, Start Bootstrap) are simply packaged sets of these same overrides.

q.en: What are Bootstrap utilities?

a.en: Tiny single-purpose CSS classes (margin, colour, border...) applied in HTML instead of writing custom CSS.

q.en: Give four benefits of using utilities.

a.en: No custom CSS files, faster development, consistent values from Bootstrap's scale, and responsive versions for many utilities.

q.en: What does mt-3 mean?

a.en: Margin-Top of size 3 = 1rem. m = margin, t = top, 3 = third step of the spacing scale.

q.en: What are the spacing sizes 0 to 5?

a.en: 0, 0.25rem, 0.5rem, 1rem, 1.5rem and 3rem; "auto" also exists for margins.

q.en: What do s and e mean in ms-2, pe-3?

a.en: Start and end: s = left, e = right (Bootstrap 4 used l and r).

q.en: What does mx-auto do?

a.en: Sets left and right margins to auto, centring a block element that has a width.

q.en: What is gap-3 used for?

a.en: Equal 1rem space between items of a flex or grid container; row-gap and column-gap set one direction only.

q.en: Differentiate w-50 and mw-100.

a.en: w-50 fixes the width to 50% of the parent; mw-100 only limits the width to never exceed the parent (max-width: 100%).

q.en: When does h-50 work?

a.en: Only when the parent element has a height set; percentages are relative to the parent's height.

q.en: What are vh-100 and vw-100?

a.en: 100% of the viewport height and width, used for full-screen sections.

q.en: What is .ratio-16x9?

a.en: A box that keeps a 16:9 aspect ratio on any screen, used for videos and iframes.

q.en: List some display values available as utilities.

a.en: none, inline, inline-block, block, table, flex, inline-flex, grid.

q.en: How do you hide an element only on phones?

a.en: d-none d-sm-block (or d-md-block) - hidden below the breakpoint, shown above.

q.en: d-none vs invisible?

a.en: d-none removes the element from the layout; invisible hides it but keeps its space (visibility: hidden).

q.en: What is .visually-hidden for?

a.en: Content hidden from sighted users but still read by screen readers (accessibility).

q.en: What are d-print-none and d-print-block?

a.en: Print utilities: they show or hide content specifically in the printed output.

q.en: Why does position-absolute need a relative parent?

a.en: An absolutely positioned element is placed relative to the nearest ancestor with position: relative (or any non-static position).

q.en: Write classes to place a badge on a button's top-right corner.

a.en: Button: position-relative; badge: position-absolute top-0 start-100 translate-middle.

q.en: What does translate-middle do?

a.en: Translates the element by -50% of its own width and height, so top-50 start-50 centres it exactly.

q.en: What is z-3 used for?

a.en: z-index stacking: elements with higher z-index values are drawn on top of overlapping elements.

q.en: List five flexbox direction and alignment classes.

a.en: flex-row, flex-column, justify-content-center (main axis), align-items-end (cross axis), flex-wrap.

q.en: justify-content vs align-items?

a.en: justify-content spaces items along the main axis; align-items aligns them on the cross axis.

q.en: What are space-between, space-around and space-evenly?

a.en: justify-content values: largest gaps only between items / equal space inside and half outside / equal space everywhere.

q.en: How do you stack items on a phone but show a row from tablets?

a.en: d-flex flex-column flex-md-row.

q.en: What do order-md-2 and flex-grow-1 do?

a.en: order-md-2 moves the item later from md up; flex-grow-1 makes the item take the container's free space.

q.en: How does ms-auto help in a flex row?

a.en: Auto margin pushes that item and everything after it to the far side (e.g. logout button at the right).

q.en: Why set border before border-danger?

a.en: The border utility creates the 1px edge; colour utilities only recolour an existing border.

q.en: Difference between rounded-pill and rounded-circle?

a.en: Pill rounds any rectangle into a capsule; circle needs equal width and height to make a perfect circle.

q.en: What does text-bg-* do?

a.en: Bootstrap 5.3 class that sets the background colour AND a contrasting text colour in one class.

q.en: bg-opacity-25 vs opacity-25?

a.en: bg-opacity-25 fades only the background; opacity-25 fades the whole element including its text.

q.en: What are bg-*-subtle and text-*-emphasis?

a.en: Soft background tints with matching readable text colours, for gentle highlight panels (Bootstrap 5.3).

q.en: overflow-auto vs overflow-hidden?

a.en: Auto shows scroll bars only when content overflows; hidden clips the overflowing content with no scrolling.

q.en: What must an overflow box have to work?

a.en: A fixed height or width, otherwise the box just grows with its content.

q.en: Which shadow utilities exist?

a.en: shadow-none, shadow-sm, shadow and shadow-lg.

q.en: What is the breakpoint infix rule?

a.en: {utility}-{sm|md|lg|xl|xxl}-{value}; the base class applies everywhere and the breakpoint class overrides from that width up.

q.en: Which utilities are NOT responsive by default?

a.en: Widths and heights (w-*, h-*), colours, borders and shadows; design has not been compiled with them; use a custom class or the Sass utility API.

q.en: Why is Bootstrap called mobile first?

a.en: Styles apply to the smallest screens by default and md/lg media queries only ADD changes for larger screens.

q.en: Why customize Bootstrap at all?

a.en: For brand identity, smaller CSS, automatic site-wide updates from one variable and design consistency.

q.en: What are Bootstrap CSS variables? Examples.

a.en: Custom properties on :root: --bs-primary, --bs-primary-rgb, --bs-body-font-family, --bs-border-radius; overriding them restyles the site at runtime.

q.en: Why override --bs-primary-rgb too?

a.en: Many effects (shadows, semi-transparent fills) build the colour from the RGB triplet, so both must stay in sync.

q.en: Where is Sass used in Bootstrap customization?

a.en: Bootstrap's source is Sass; its defaults are variables with !default that our custom file overrides, then a compiler (Dart Sass) builds a custom bootstrap.css.

q.en: What does !default mean in Sass?

a.en: "Use this value only if it is not already set" - so our variables written before the import always win.

q.en: Where should custom Sass variables be placed?

a.en: Before the @import of Bootstrap in the custom .scss file.

q.en: What is a Sass partial?

a.en: A .scss file whose name starts with an underscore; it is imported into other files and not compiled on its own.

q.en: How do you compile Sass to CSS?

a.en: With Dart Sass: dart-sass input.scss output.css, usually through an npm build script.

q.en: What are component variables? Give two.

a.en: Variables that tune one component: e.g. $card-border-radius, $btn-border-radius, $navbar-padding-y.

q.en: What is a Sass map in Bootstrap?

a.en: A key-value list like $theme-colors; adding a key with map-merge creates every utility and component variant for that colour.

q.en: What does map-merge($theme-colors, ("brand": #7b1fa2)) create?

a.en: btn-brand, alert-brand, bg-brand, text-brand, border-brand and friends, with proper hover and contrast states.

q.en: How do you make the compiled CSS smaller?

a.en: Remove unused colours with map-remove and import only the needed Bootstrap modules.

q.en: What is a Bootstrap theme?

a.en: A packaged set of variable and component overrides (colours, radius, shadows, fonts) giving the site a consistent identity.

q.en: How do you enable dark mode in Bootstrap 5.3?

a.en: Set data-bs-theme="dark" on the html element or on any section; all components adapt automatically.

q.en: How do you build a custom colour mode?

a.en: Define a [data-bs-theme="name"] selector that overrides the CSS variables, then apply the attribute where wanted.

q.en: What rule keeps markup themable?

a.en: Use semantic classes (btn-primary, text-bg-primary, bg-body) and never hard-coded hex colours, so themes can restyle everything.
